articles.title: Integrierte Browser: So helfen dir Claude Cowork und ChatGPT Work bei Logins und mehr
articles.text:
Claude Cowork und ChatGPT Work: Warum der neue Browser-Zugang so praktisch ist
Der Web-Zugriff von Claude Cowork und ChatGPT Work läuft jetzt einfacher denn je. Aufgaben, die du an Anthropics und OpenAIs Allround-Agents weitergibst, können mithilfe der integrierten Browser auch Kontexte wie Web-Zugriffe oder Logins beinhalten. Du musst in diesem Fall nicht mehr selbst einen Login über deinen eigenen Browser vornehmen, sondern kannst einfach die Agents arbeiten lassen. Das ermöglicht umfassende Praxisanwendungen für den Alltag. Diese unterstützt Claude Cowork zudem mit einer optimierten Erinnerung.
In Claude Cowork ist jetzt ein Browser integriert. Du musst ihn nicht eigens installieren, er ist in die Desktop-App integriert. Dieser Browser ist von deinem eigenen Browser samt Logindaten getrennt. Alle zahlenden User können diesen integrierten Browser oder Claude in Chrome als Agent-Browser-Kombination nutzen, die inzwischen umfassend verfügbar ist. Claude in Chrome bleibt für alle, die es schon nutzen, als Default eingestellt.
Der neue integrierte Browser in Cowork kann indes Websites navigieren, wenn diese im Rahmen einer Aufgabe angesteuert werden sollen oder müssen. Dabei kann der Agent im Browser Dokumente ausfüllen und weitere Aufgaben aus einem Sidepanel heraus übernehmen. Diese Option kommt für Pro, Max und Team-User.
Sicherheit und Datenschutz bei automatisierten Web-Logins
Nutzer:innen sollten unterscheiden, welchen Browser-Zugang sie benötigen. Oft braucht es für eine Aufgabe nur irgendeinen Browser, keinen mit persönlichen Login-Details oder Lesezeichen. User können ihre Login-Daten aus anderen Browsern allerdings übertragen, falls gewünscht, wobei Banking-Seiten, E‑Mail-Logins und Single Sign-ons per Default erstmal ausgeschlossen sind. In den Einstellungen können die User jederzeit ändern, wie sie mit Claude Cowork auf das Web zugreifen möchten.
ChatGPT Work: Web-Automatisierung für Business-Prozesse
Den Web-Zugriff erleichtert auch ChatGPT Work. Der Agent kann jetzt auf einen eigenen Browser und Computer zugreifen, um Logins im Web und auch mobil vorzunehmen. Dabei soll ChatGPT niemals die Passwörter oder Logindaten sehen. Plus, Pro und Business-User können mit der neuen Funktion webbasierte Aufgaben mit ChatGPT Work abdecken, die einen Login und normalerweise eine eigenständige Browser-Bedienung erfordern. Dazu zählen Aufgaben wie das Finden von Wohnungen zu den eigenen Suchkriterien einer Wohnungssuche, das Absagen von Terminen bei Restaurants, Praxen und Co., die Erledigung von Papierkram für Versicherungsfragen oder der automatisierte Online-Einkauf auf Basis hochgeladener Bilder.
Claude Cowork mit Erinnerungs-Boost: Details aus dem Chat als Basis für Aufgaben
Damit du Claude Cowork nicht immer neu detailliert erklären musst, wie eine Aufgabe aussieht, kannst du künftig aus allen Chats mit Claude schöpfen. Denn Anthropic verbindet die Erinnerungen vom Chat mit Claude und Claude Cowork. Das heißt, Aufgaben für Claude Cowork können auf Basis von Details aus früheren Chats erstellt und schnell gestartet werden. Das ist hilfreich, falls schon einmal Präferenzen oder Ideen, auch von Kund:innen, Mitarbeiter:innen und Co., geteilt wurden.
KI-Gedächtnis: Personalisierte Workflows durch User-Kontrolle
Die User behalten aber die volle Kontrolle darüber, was in diesen Erinnerungen auftaucht. In den Einstellungen findet sich eine Liste der gespeicherten Themen. Dort können User einzelne Elemente entfernen, bearbeiten oder noch einmal nachlesen. Spezifische Elemente lassen sich zudem mit dem Prompt „remember this“ hervorheben. In den Erinnerungen tauchen einige Themen allerdings nicht auf. Dazu zählen Details zur Religionszugehörigkeit, Gesundheit und dergleichen. Sie können aktiv integriert werden, sind aber per Default von der Speicherung ausgenommen.
Der Artikel stammt von Niklas Lewanczik aus der OnlineMarketing.de-Redaktion und wird im Rahmen einer Content-Kooperation auf t3n veröffentlicht.

articles.title: Deepgram deepens Amazon SageMaker AI observability with Enhanced Metrics | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Deepgram deepens Amazon SageMaker AI observability with Enhanced Metrics
Self-hosted speech AI has historically carried an observability trade-off. The service can tell you an endpoint is up and how many requests it served. The questions that actually drive capacity planning and cost management stay locked inside the vendor’s container: what you are billed for, which features your traffic uses, and what the inference engine is doing on each GPU.
If you run Deepgram’s speech-to-text (STT) and text-to-speech (TTS) models on SageMaker AI, audio and transcripts stay inside your own AWS account. This can help support your data residency and compliance efforts without giving up a managed control plane for deployment, scaling, and monitoring. Your specific obligations depend on your own controls and assessments, so consult your compliance team and review the AWS shared responsibility model.
Deepgram is closing the gap on billing, feature usage, and engine behavior with the following two innovations, available today on Deepgram SageMaker AI deployments.
- Deepgram Enhanced Metrics: Usage and billing metrics that the Deepgram container publishes directly into your Amazon CloudWatch account, with no agent, no sidecar, and no additional IAM permissions. These are the same consumed-unit values that drive AWS Marketplace metered billing, so you can reconcile your AWS bill against actual traffic down to the model and transport.
- Prometheus and OpenTelemetry support: Engine-level Prometheus metrics scraped straight from the Deepgram container, and per-GPU accelerator and host metrics. Both are collected through SageMaker AI detailed observability and queryable with PromQL from CloudWatch, Grafana, or any Prometheus-compatible tool.
In this post, we walk through both capabilities: how they work, what they show you that you couldn’t see before, and how to start using them on a Deepgram SageMaker AI endpoint.
Deepgram on Amazon SageMaker AI
Deepgram’s speech models are available as model packages on AWS Marketplace and deploy as SageMaker AI real-time endpoints in your account. With SageMaker AI, you get baseline observability on your endpoints automatically: invocation metrics such as ConcurrentRequestsPerModel and FirstChunkLatency in CloudWatch, container logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and alarm-driven automatic scaling.
AWS Marketplace model packages run with network isolation. The container cannot make outbound connections, which is why security-conscious customers choose this deployment model. The same isolation, however, is what normally makes vendor-level telemetry hard. The container can’t push metrics to an external collector, and you can’t see inside the container. Both capabilities in this post work within that constraint: neither requires the container to open a network path, and both land the data in your own CloudWatch account.
        A note on terminology: SageMaker AI has its own endpoint feature called enhanced metrics (EnableEnhancedMetrics in MetricsConfig), which adds per-instance and per-GPU utilization dimensions to the standard endpoint metrics. The SageMaker AI feature is distinct from and complementary to Deepgram Enhanced Metrics, the Deepgram-published billing and usage metrics described in the following sections. This post covers the Deepgram capability. For the SageMaker AI capability, see Deepgram’s SageMaker observability guide.
Innovation 1: Billing and usage transparency with Deepgram Enhanced Metrics
Deepgram Enhanced Metrics answer two questions no standard endpoint metric can: exactly what you’re being billed for, and how your traffic actually uses Deepgram’s features.
How it works: Metrics that ride the logging path
The Deepgram container writes CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) records to container stdout. SageMaker AI already forwards container output to the endpoint’s CloudWatch log group, and CloudWatch Logs extracts EMF records into metrics automatically. The EMF path gives you the following benefits.
- No agent, sidecar, or collector to deploy.
- No additional IAM permissions beyond what the endpoint already has for logging.
- Works under AWS Marketplace network isolation, because metrics travel over the existing SageMaker-to-CloudWatch logging path rather than any outbound network connection.
- Classic CloudWatch metrics: They appear in aws cloudwatch list-metrics and work withget-metric-statistics , dashboards, alarms, and metric math, with nothing to enable on the endpoint configuration.
All dimensions are low-cardinality and contain no personally identifiable information (PII): no transcripts, TTS input, or per-request identifiers.
Deepgram Enhanced Metrics aggregate across the Deepgram endpoints in your AWS account and Region. The dimensions cover category, model, and transport, but not endpoint name or instance ID, so you cannot filter this stream to a single endpoint or instance. For per-endpoint, per-instance, or per-GPU breakdowns, use the Prometheus and OpenTelemetry metrics in the next section.
Reconcile your AWS Marketplace bill: The Deepgram/SageMakerInference namespace
The billing namespace emits one record per completed request, covering each streaming session, pre-recorded request, and TTS request. The ConsumedUnits metric carries the same billable-unit values that drive AWS Marketplace metered billing. The following table lists the metrics this namespace publishes.
| Metric | Unit | Description | 
| ConsumedUnits | Count | Billable inference units for the request. Sum over a period is the total billed volume. | 
| AudioDurationSeconds | Seconds | Duration of audio processed (speech-to-text). | 
| CharCount | Count | Characters synthesized (text-to-speech). | 
Dimensions are published at three granularities ([Category], [Category, Model], and [Category, Model, Transport]), so you can answer what did streaming STT cost this month and how much of that was nova-3 with the same namespace. For example, total consumed units per hour for streaming speech-to-text:
SampleCount is the number of billed requests. Because these are ordinary CloudWatch metrics, you can build a finance-facing billing dashboard or set a budget alarm on consumed units.
Understand how your endpoint is used: The Deepgram/SelfHosted namespace
A second stream, emitted by the Deepgram API server itself, breaks raw usage down by method, model tier, and enabled feature, independent of billing. It answers product-level questions: how much traffic is streaming versus pre-recorded, which model tiers process the most audio, and which features (diarization, smart formatting, redaction, keyterm prompting) your applications actually enable. The following table lists the metrics in this namespace and the dimensions each one carries.
| Metric | Dimensions | What it tells you | 
| AudioMs ,Requests | Deployment ,Method | Volume by streaming compared to pre-recorded | 
| TierAudioMs | Deployment ,Tier | Audio processed per model tier (for example, nova-3 ,flux ) | 
| FeatureAudioMs ,FeatureTokens | Deployment ,Feature | Utilization per enabled feature (for example, diarize ,smart_format ,redact ) | 
| TtsCharacters ,Tokens ,VoiceAgentMs | Deployment ,Method | TTS, intelligence-feature, and voice-agent volume | 
For example, how much audio ran with diarization enabled in the last 24 hours:
The usage stream is on by default and can be disabled with a single environment variable override in the endpoint configuration (DEEPGRAM_API_01: emf.enabled=false). The billing stream cannot be disabled. It is part of the metering pipeline.
Innovation 2: Engine-level and per-GPU visibility with Prometheus and OpenTelemetry
Deepgram containers serve a Prometheus metrics endpoint, and SageMaker AI detailed observability runs an AWS managed OpenTelemetry Collector on each instance backing the endpoint. The collector scrapes the container and exports the results to CloudWatch, and it exports per-GPU and host-level metrics.
With detailed observability enabled, three metric sources publish to the CloudWatch OTel-compatible metric store. The following table describes each source and why it matters.
| Source | Example metrics | Why it matters | 
| GPU (DCGM exporter) | DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL ,DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED | Per-GPU series. On multi-GPU instances, each GPU reports separately, so a saturated device can’t hide behind a summed or averaged utilization number. | 
| Host (node exporter) | node_cpu_seconds_total ,node_memory_MemTotal_bytes | Standard Prometheus node-exporter metrics for each instance. | 
| Deepgram engine | engine_active_requests{kind="stream"} ,engine_estimated_stream_capacity | The collector scrapes the Deepgram container’s Prometheus endpoint directly. These are the same API and Engine metrics Deepgram’s self-hosted customers use for capacity planning, now available on SageMaker AI without running any collector yourself. See Deepgram’s Metrics Guide for the complete reference. | 
engine_estimated_stream_capacity is the Deepgram engine’s own estimate of how many concurrent streams the instance can sustain. Comparing it against engine_active_requests gives you an engine-reported headroom signal for scaling decisions.
Every series carries SageMaker resource labels, including aws.sagemaker.endpoint.name, the variant name, and the instance ID. You can filter to a single endpoint, isolate one instance in a scaled-out fleet, or compare GPUs within an instance. Because the collector runs on the host, outside the model container, this works under AWS Marketplace network isolation.
Enabling it
Detailed observability is on by default for newly created endpoints, publishing every 60 seconds. To set it explicitly, for example on an endpoint created before the feature launched, or to change the publish frequency, use MetricsConfig on the endpoint configuration:
For an endpoint already serving traffic, create a new endpoint configuration and run update-endpoint. The update is a blue/green deployment, and the endpoint stays in service.
Query with PromQL from CloudWatch, Grafana, or anything Prometheus-compatible
The metrics land in the CloudWatch OTel metric store and are queried with PromQL. In the CloudWatch console’s PromQL editor, filter per-GPU utilization to one endpoint:
CloudWatch also exposes a standard Prometheus-compatible HTTP API for these metrics, authenticated with SigV4:
If you’ve standardized on Grafana or another Prometheus-native observability stack, you can point your existing tooling at your SageMaker AI fleet: no parallel monitoring stack, no export pipeline.
Choosing the right metric stream
The two innovations complement the built-in metrics of SageMaker AI rather than replacing them. The following table maps common questions to the metric stream that answers them.
| Question | Where to look | 
| Is the endpoint healthy? Are requests erroring or slow to start? | Standard SageMaker metrics ( ConcurrentRequestsPerModel ,FirstChunkLatency ,Invocation5XXErrors ) | 
| What is my Marketplace bill going to be, and which models drove it? | Deepgram Enhanced Metrics ( Deepgram/SageMakerInference , account-level) | 
| Which features and model tiers does my traffic actually use? | Deepgram Enhanced Metrics ( Deepgram/SelfHosted , account-level) | 
| How saturated is each GPU? How much stream capacity remains on each instance of a specific endpoint? | Prometheus/OTel through detailed observability (DCGM and Deepgram engine metrics, per endpoint/instance/GPU) | 
Get started
Deepgram Enhanced Metrics require no setup: they flow into your CloudWatch account from the moment a Deepgram SageMaker AI endpoint serves traffic. Detailed observability is on by default for new endpoints and takes one endpoint-configuration change to add to existing ones. To get started, use the following resources.
- Deploy Deepgram from AWS Marketplace and follow Deploy Deepgram on Amazon SageMaker.
- Reference: Deepgram Enhanced Metrics, Prometheus & OpenTelemetry Metrics, and the Metrics Guide for the complete list of Deepgram API and Engine metrics.
- AWS documentation: Detailed observability for SageMaker AI endpoints.
Conclusion
Self-hosting speech AI no longer leaves a gap between the service’s request counters and the vendor’s invoice. Deepgram Enhanced Metrics land the exact units that drive AWS Marketplace billing in your own CloudWatch account, with zero infrastructure. The feature-level usage behind those units lands there too. With Prometheus and OpenTelemetry support through SageMaker AI detailed observability, the Deepgram engine’s own capacity and load metrics and per-GPU utilization are one PromQL query away in the tools your team already uses.
These capabilities are Deepgram’s latest investment in SageMaker AI as a preferred deployment option for self-hosted speech AI, following IAM Temporary Delegation for support access. They continue the commitment of making the day-two experience match the day-one experience. Deepgram models currently listed on SageMaker AI, including Nova, Flux, and Aura-2, come with a 14-day trial at no additional cost. Your team can stand up a real deployment in your own AWS account before committing. Running Deepgram models on SageMaker AI incurs charges for endpoint hosting, including GPU instances. It also incurs charges for Amazon CloudWatch logs and metrics and associated networking resources. While the Deepgram trial is offered at no additional cost, AWS infrastructure costs apply from the start of deployment. Review the SageMaker AI pricing and use AWS Cost Explorer to monitor your spending.

articles.title: ¿Cómo funciona el mercado de criptomonedas y cuál es su valor este jueves 27 de agosto?
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
PUBLICIDAD
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 78.761,68 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de -0,336% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de -0,644% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.490,12 dólares.
PUBLICIDAD
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0,02%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 705,36 dólares, con un cambio de 1,63%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 49.8 dólares, tras una variación de -0.2369985.
PUBLICIDAD
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,09 dólares tras presentar un cambio de 1,38% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
PUBLICIDAD
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
PUBLICIDAD
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
PUBLICIDAD
Criptomonedas en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
PUBLICIDAD
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
PUBLICIDAD
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: GTA 6 revela gameplay: assaltos planejados, mundo aberto e romance entre Jason e Lucia
articles.text:
A Rockstar Games finalmente apresentou um olhar mais aprofundado sobre a jogabilidade de Grand Theft Auto VI. Exibido nesta quinta-feira (27) primeiro pela Netflix, Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look mostrou diferentes sistemas de gameplay, novas regiões do mapa e mais detalhes sobre a história de Jason Duval e Lucia Caminos.
O material reforça que a relação entre os dois protagonistas estará diretamente ligada à trama criminal. A descrição oficial do jogo já indicava que Jason e Lucia acabam envolvidos em uma conspiração que atravessa o estado de Leonida depois que um serviço dá errado.
Agora, a nova apresentação ajuda a mostrar como essa história deve funcionar na prática.
Jason e Lucia entram de vez no mundo do crime
O gameplay mostra Jason e Lucia envolvidos com uma organização criminosa e apresenta Raul Bautista, personagem que assume uma posição próxima à de mentor da dupla.
Raul já havia sido apresentado anteriormente como um criminoso experiente, associado principalmente a grandes roubos e sempre em busca de pessoas dispostas a assumir riscos maiores. No novo material, essa experiência parece servir para colocar Jason e Lucia em operações progressivamente mais complexas.
A dupla passa a integrar o grupo comandado pelo criminoso, abrindo caminho para missões envolvendo diferentes organizações e conflitos entre gangues.
Ao mesmo tempo, a Rockstar dedica espaço ao romance entre Jason e Lucia, indicando que a relação dos protagonistas não funcionará apenas como pano de fundo para os crimes.
Assaltos parecem mais elaborados em GTA 6
Uma das partes que mais chama atenção é a estrutura dos crimes.
Em vez de apresentar somente roubos improvisados, o vídeo mostra operações com planejamento prévio, invasões, confrontos armados e fugas carregando sacos de dinheiro.
Há também uma sequência envolvendo uma casa utilizada para fabricação de drogas que rapidamente se transforma em uma grande confusão, reforçando o papel das organizações criminosas na história.
A impressão deixada pela apresentação é que alguns dos grandes assaltos poderão exigir preparação antes da execução, aproveitando ideias que já estavam presentes em GTA V, mas aparentemente com mais possibilidades.
Jogador poderá alternar entre Jason e Lucia
Outra característica de GTA V que retorna é a possibilidade de alternar entre protagonistas.
Desta vez, o sistema é utilizado para acompanhar Jason e Lucia durante diferentes momentos das missões. Isso permite que uma mesma operação seja vista ou executada de perspectivas diferentes.
A seleção de armas também mantém uma estrutura visual semelhante à utilizada no título anterior, facilitando a troca de equipamentos durante confrontos.
Tiroteios podem causar danos visíveis aos carros
O combate aparece em diferentes momentos da apresentação, incluindo confrontos dentro e fora dos veículos.
Durante perseguições, é possível atirar contra outros carros, enquanto os veículos parecem reagir aos impactos sofrendo danos visíveis durante o confronto.
A Rockstar também mostrou novamente seu sistema de perseguição policial. Um elemento clássico da franquia retorna: o mapa começa a piscar quando policiais estão se aproximando da região, ajudando o jogador a identificar o perigo durante uma fuga.
Carros continuam sendo parte importante de GTA
Como esperado, dirigir continua sendo uma das principais atividades de Grand Theft Auto VI.
O vídeo mostra Jason e Lucia atravessando diferentes regiões de Vice City e Leonida, participando de corridas e perseguições, além de apresentar opções de personalização de veículos.
As cenas também ajudam a dimensionar o mapa. Além das áreas urbanas de Vice City, aparecem praias, estradas e regiões montanhosas que podem favorecer atividades como corridas off-road e rali.
A Rockstar já havia confirmado que a história se passa no estado fictício de Leonida, inspirado na Flórida, tendo Vice City como uma de suas principais cidades.
GTA 6 terá atividades para além das missões
Nem tudo envolve cometer crimes. A apresentação mostrou diversas atividades que poderão ser realizadas enquanto o jogador explora o mundo aberto.
Entre elas estão natação, jet ski, basquete, corridas de carro e salto de paraquedas.
A presença dessas atividades sugere que a Rockstar pretende novamente transformar o mapa em um espaço que pode ser explorado independentemente da campanha principal.
O mar também parece ter importância maior. Além de nadar, os personagens podem utilizar diferentes veículos aquáticos, aproveitando a extensa região costeira de Leonida.
Vice City está maior e mais detalhada
O novo gameplay também dedicou bastante tempo à apresentação dos cenários.
A Rockstar mostrou uma extensa área do mapa, passando pela cidade, praias e regiões mais afastadas. A variedade de ambientes indica que GTA 6 não ficará restrito às ruas de Vice City.
Negócios e estabelecimentos também continuam presentes pelo mapa, mantendo uma característica tradicional da franquia e aumentando a quantidade de lugares que podem ser encontrados durante a exploração.
Mais do que apresentar apenas o tamanho do cenário, o vídeo sugere uma preocupação em tornar esses espaços parte das atividades disponíveis ao jogador.
GTA 6 parece expandir a fórmula de GTA 5
A apresentação não indica uma ruptura completa com aquilo que funcionou em Grand Theft Auto V. Sistemas conhecidos, como a roda de seleção de armas, perseguições policiais, troca entre protagonistas, direção e atividades paralelas continuam presentes.
A principal diferença parece estar na profundidade e no nível de interação desses sistemas.
Carros apresentam danos durante confrontos, crimes parecem envolver planos mais elaborados, Jason e Lucia desempenham funções diferentes nas operações e o mundo oferece atividades que vão de corridas a esportes e exploração aquática.
Tudo isso acontece enquanto a Rockstar desenvolve a relação entre os protagonistas e sua entrada em uma estrutura criminosa maior.

articles.title: Plaud's new earphones come with an eSIM-enabled case for talking to AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Hardware companies have realized that note-taking is one of the easiest AI use cases to build for, and consequently have been busy shoving mics into everything from pendants and rings to credit-card-sized pucks and wristbands. Still, despite the variety of devices, only a few companies have been able to stand out.
One of these companies is Plaud, which has over 2.5 million people using its hardware or software. It is now launching a note-taker in a new form factor: earphones. Called Plaud One, these adopt the simple bare-bones style of Apple’s AirPods, and can record calls, while their case can be used to record in-person conversations or take notes.
Plaud isn’t the first to this form factor. Its rivals Viaim and Anker already have similar note-taking earbuds in the market.
But the company is betting on its software and AI chops to set these apart. Plaud said that once the earbuds transcribe your conversation, its AI agent — which can connect to tools like Gmail, Google Calendar, Notion, and Slack — can do things like writing follow-up emails and creating documents or presentations based on the contents of the conversation.
By itself, that isn’t a unique pitch. Software note-takers like Granola, Fathom, and Read AI have been offering similar workflow automation for a while now, transcribing calls and conversations, and allowing you to subsequently get an AI agent to do various tasks.
The Plaud One takes that a step further, though, with its case, which supports an eSIM card. That feature, the company says, allows users to instruct Plaud’s AI agents remotely without using their phone or computer.
The Plaud One has 12mm drivers and features active noise cancellation. The company says the case can capture voices clearly within a range of five meters, and the earphones can record six hours of in-person meetings and three hours of calls on a single charge. Combined with the case, users can record up to 25 hours of conversations on a single charge.
Buyers get 300 minutes of free transcription per month, after which they will need to buy additional plans, which start from $8.33 per month (paid annually).
That said, this launch seems to be more of a trial run. The Plaud One will be limited in quantity, as the startup likely wants to gauge demand for such AI-focused earphones before it commits to the format.
Plaud is also working on building agentic capabilities, which is expected to arrive as part of an update in the coming months. The company says it will introduce a credit-based system for different tasks, and buyers of the Plaud One will get $200 in credits for these tasks.
The company has had a good run so far, claiming in June that it had reached annual run-rate revenue of $100 million. However, competition in the market is intense, with new hardware note-takers releasing every week. Its rival, YC-backed Pocket, has also reached that milestone, and tons of other companies like Anker, Comu, Viaim, and software startup Genspark are building in the space.
Plaud’s CEO Nathan Xu holds that there should be an interface to talk to AI to invoke it from anywhere, and earbuds meet that need.
“[For AI] we need to have a wearable and an always-ready interface, one that people love to wear, is socially acceptable, and private by design,” he said in a briefing.
Still, the company may find it challenging to draw people away from using their AirPods, Google Pixel Buds, Samsung Galaxy Buds, or wireless earbuds from any number of audio companies, which can pretty much do the same job when paired with any note-taking app.
Xu says Plaud is not necessarily competing against these companies, but positioning its meeting-recording tech to adopt a popular wearable format.
Users can preorder the device now for $249, and it will ship in the fourth quarter of 2026.

articles.title: Americans are cheering for vigilantes who take down Flock cameras
articles.text:
Americans have declared war on Flock cameras. They’ve protested them, damaged them, and destroyed them. This is only the beginning.
Americans are cheering for vigilantes who take down Flock cameras
The surveillance cameras have become another flashpoint of growing bipartisan anger against tech industry excess.
The spontaneous and decentralized nature of the vigilante protests is also what makes them difficult to suppress. There isn’t a uniform method of disruption; people have done everything from unplugging, smashing, stealing, and spray-painting the surveillance devices to taking less destructive actions like physically blocking the cameras for hours. Some of the culprits have been caught, but that clearly hasn’t dissuaded others from taking matters into their own hands.
“Nonviolent direct action is a recognized and established tactic, and it’s unsurprising that we are seeing some people are resorting to that.”
Support for those taking drastic measures to get rid of the cameras has also become commonplace online. Last week, a police sheriff in Lumpkin County, Georgia, took to Facebook to announce a $1,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of whoever destroyed a Flock Safety camera installed near a local park. “I hope you’re happy with this. It was to keep our kids safe,” Sheriff Stacy Jarrard said in a video, admonishing the unknown perpetrators while unintentionally confirming what many people already knew: Police are using the cameras to do a lot more than simply give out speeding tickets.
The response was not what he was expecting. Jarrard’s post has since received more than 30,000 comments, the vast majority opposing the cameras and many mocking the police and even praising the vandals. “Looks like a Constitutional wind blew it over,” taunted one commenter. “Looks like somebody fixed it for you guys,” wrote another. Others congratulated the culprits, saying those taking direct action to remove the cameras in towns and cities across the US are “doing the lord’s work.” In response to the backlash, Jarrard changed his tone, posting a new video that admitted the need for privacy measures, but stopped short of promising the cameras would be taken down. “We need more safeguards in motion,” Jarrard said. “I’m going to listen to you.”
A few weeks earlier, in suburban New York, police reported a rash of vandalism against Flock cameras in Long Island’s Suffolk County, where four of the cameras had been unplugged, spray-painted, and run over with a car. An article about the incidents in the conservative publication New York Post also attracted a mass of comments opposing the cameras and supporting the people who destroyed them. “They’ve tried to put them up by my house, but someone keeps running them over,” one reader commented on the Post article. “I bet they have gone through a dozen, so far. Thanks to whoever is doing it.”
Support for Flock vigilantes has gone beyond internet comments. In one recent case, an Air Force engineer accused of cutting down 13 Flock cameras in Virginia has received over $44,000 for his legal defense from supporters via GoFundMe. In another, felony charges against an alleged Flock vandal in Ohio were dismissed after a grand jury declined to indict the suspect.
The fact that so many people seem to not only oppose the cameras but openly support those stealing and destroying them is a historically significant milestone for the anti-Big Tech movement. Activist historians often refer to this approach as a “diversity of tactics” — the idea that movements become stronger when they tolerate those taking extralegal direct action and reject narratives that divide them into “good” and “bad” protesters. As author Margaret Killjoy recently argued in a piece about Flock vandalism: “Social movements are effective specifically when there is solidarity between their broader base and the people who are committing criminal direct action. When social movements stand behind their criminals, they win.”
Flock camera destruction isn’t just popular — in some cases, it has also proven highly effective at getting rid of them. Earlier this month, police in Winona, Minnesota, said they would not reinstall the city’s eight Flock cameras after all of them were stolen, citing “growing concerns about trust in policing.” On August 3rd, following two incidents where Flock cameras were destroyed, police in Burnet County, Texas, announced that they had removed all Flock cameras from the area.
Like the widespread resistance to AI data centers, support for anti-Flock vigilantism is part of a rapidly growing public sentiment that cuts across geography and political allegiances. The cameras, which have been heavily criticized for their widespread abuse and for being deployed without public hearings or community approval, have quickly become another populist flashpoint of a growing bipartisan movement against tech industry excess. From coastal urban sprawls to rural areas in deep-red states, the message is clear: Folks absolutely despise these things and want them gone by any means necessary.
“Nonviolent direct action is a recognized and established tactic, and it’s unsurprising that we are seeing some people are resorting to that,” Alex Marthews, national chair of the nonprofit civil rights group Restore the Fourth, told The Verge. “They’re doing so because the whole structure for approval of surveillance technologies like this has been set up to minimize peoples’ control. Everything gets arranged by public safety people for public safety people, with an explicit intent of shutting the public out. ... What do they expect to happen?” (Flock Safety did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.)
While Flock was initially advertised as an automatic license plate reader system (ALPR), in practice the AI-powered cameras are frequently used by police to track individual vehicles and people based on a wide range of identifying characteristics. In the past month alone, 18 cops in Georgia have been arrested for misusing Flock cameras. A steady stream of media stories has exposed police officers around the country who were stalking their romantic interests, spouses, and other innocent people using the cameras.
“It’s not just that they see the camera and take it down. Even when the people who destroy these cameras are caught, there’s a public intrigue to it.”
“People are seeing these cameras in their communities. They are hearing stories of police using them to stalk people. They are reading stories of the tech being used to target immigrants and people exercising their First Amendment rights — and folks are connecting the dots,” Chris Gilliard, an independent privacy researcher and author of the forthcoming book Luxury Surveillance, told The Verge.
There still isn’t any scientific data measuring the opposition to Flock nationwide, but smaller polls conducted by research groups and local media outlets show overwhelming opposition to the cameras. According to a recent poll by Spry Research in rural Tennessee’s Knox County, 58 percent of voters say they oppose Flock cameras, and half believe they violate the Fourth Amendment. And in an online poll by NBC News affiliate WJAR in Providence, Rhode Island, 83 percent said they opposed the deployment of Flock cameras in their city or town.
Politicians are beginning to catch on, including those from red states. Last month, a trio of House Republicans led by Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) introduced a bill to prohibit the federal government from purchasing Flock cameras or similar technology. Republicans in Pennsylvania and West Virginia have put out statements opposing the cameras, with the former urging constituents to call their representatives and tell them to “Stop the Flock.” Legislation that would put warrant restrictions on Flock cameras or ban them outright has been proposed in multiple states, including Maine, Michigan, and Texas. And a man who was running for a seat in the Tennessee House of Representatives was recently arrested after allegedly shooting four different cameras with a gun.
Marthews says the bipartisan opposition to Flock across the country confounds the idea that privacy and civil rights are the exclusive purview of left-leaning communities.
“The MAGA base does not like this stuff. They do not like being intruded upon in matters intrinsic to their everyday life,” Marthews told The Verge. “If you’re talking about rural areas, you’re going to be driving everywhere. They don’t have a choice about whether to drive, and therefore they don’t have a choice about whether Flock is sucking up all this information about everywhere they go.”
Dozens of cities and counties across the US have now terminated, rejected, or declined to renew contracts with Flock Safety since the beginning of last year. In total, more than 130 cities have rejected ALPR systems, according to the site DeFlock, which maintains a map revealing the locations of Flock cameras across the country. Opposition to the technology is even impacting the real estate market — some homebuyers are using the DeFlock map to avoid buying property in areas where the cameras have been deployed. Even Flock CEO Garrett Langley has been forced to soften his stance toward anti-Flock activists. He recently apologized for comments in a previous interview where he referred to DeFlock as a “terroristic” group. He has also announced changes to the software.
Viet Trinh, a historian and professor of ethnic studies at Ohio State University who testified against Flock cameras in a recent hearing, says the public and performative nature of Flock vandalism is another aspect of its viral popularity.
“It’s not just that they see the camera and take it down. Even when the people who destroy these cameras are caught, there’s a public intrigue to it,” Trinh told The Verge. “The fact that nobody likes these cameras and that there’s someone out there willing to do something about it captures the public imagination.”
Gilliard doesn’t think it’s a coincidence that the vigilante actions against Flock cameras are occurring simultaneously with widespread protests against power-hungry data centers. In a sense, they are simply the most convenient and visible targets of a growing populist anger against Silicon Valley and its ongoing obsession with forcing AI and surveillance into every aspect of our lives. “It’s easier to deface a camera than it would be to smash Claude or ChatGPT,” said Gilliard.
Despite the recent momentum, advocates like Marthews worry that too much of the pushback is limited to Flock itself. Even now, competitors like Axon smell blood in the water, and they’re moving in to capitalize on the widespread public scrutiny of the company. It highlights what privacy advocates see as a critical vulnerability in the current tech backlash movement — the tendency to focus on one or two highly villainized companies instead of the technologies and systems themselves.
“There is this visceral understanding that this technology is a surveillance tech that more or less criminalizes anyone who drives a car or sits in a car.”
“A lot of this seems like anti-Flock rather than anti-surveillance,” said Gilliard. “Unfortunately as with most things, people often don’t feel moved unless a thing affects them personally. I think it’s an important moment because reformers are talking more and more about ‘guardrails,’ when the proper solution is abolition.”
Whatever form the pushback might take in the future, Flock has made clear that the popular anger against the tech industry isn’t confined to one political party — and those taking action aren’t being constrained by what is legal.
“There is this visceral understanding that this technology is a surveillance tech that more or less criminalizes anyone who drives a car or sits in a car,” said Trinh. “People who are on the right and normally support these punitive measures imagine that they don’t apply to them. But I think what’s happening with this tech is there’s now a very intuitive understanding that in this case, everyone is a criminal.”

articles.title: Answering your burning tech questions | BetaKit
articles.text:
Sometimes, you get what you asked for.
Honouring the podcasting ways of old, we put out a call for your burning questions on Canadian tech and tech from a Canadian perspective to produce a summer mailbag episode. Boy howdy did you deliver.
“My god. Every time I ask you people for questions, I instantly regret it.”
The submitted questions from The BetaKit Podcast audience (along with a few friends of the pod) were pointed, to say the least. What is Canada’s most overrated tech company? How do we keep young founders in the country? Can longstanding access to capital problems be solved? Is a vibrant Canadian tech ecosystem even possible?
And oh so many questions about AI.
It’s an eclectic query mix that, taken as a whole, accurately reflects the current state of tech. It’s also a veritable gauntlet for one lone podcast host to navigate, leading me to swear off mailbag episodes entirely… until the next one.
Subscribe: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, Overcast, Pocket Casts, RSS
My handwringing is just a delaying tactic to distract you from the big question: was I able to supply any useful answers to your burning tech questions?
I’ll leave that for you to decide. Let’s dig in.

articles.title: El nuevo actor de James Bond, a punto de conocerse: estos son los candidatos finales con un nuevo favorito
articles.text:
Amazon MGM Studios ya se encuentra en las fases finales para fichar al nuevo actor de James Bond. Después del final de la saga de Daniel Craig con No Time to Die, la compañía le compró a Michael G. Wilson y Barbara Broccoli el control creativo de la saga. La intención era reiniciar la franquicia con un nuevo intérprete y nuevas aventuras. De hecho, ya han anunciado a Denis Villeneuve (Dune, Blade Runner 2049) como director de la próxima película.
Sin embargo, el tiempo pasa y el nuevo actor de James Bond aún sigue sin conocerse. Aunque, según las informaciones de Page Six Hollywood, esto está a punto de cambiar. Y es que el estudio ha programado unas audiciones para principios de septiembre y, así, cerrar definitivamente el proceso y elegir al próximo intérprete del agente 007.
De hecho, de acuerdo a la misma fuente, la compañía ya tiene una lista final de candidatos. Entre ellos están Jacob Elordi (Euphoria, Frankenstein), Paul Mescal (Normal People, Gladiator II), Harris Dickinson (Triángulo de la trsiteza, El clan de hierro), Jack Lowden (Dunkerque, Slow Horses) o Callum Turner (One Night Only, Animales Fantásticos). Sin embargo, Amazon MGM Studios tendría un principal favorito.
Al parecer, el actor Jack Barton se ha convertido en el candidato principal para ser el nuevo James Bond. El intérprete británico es conocido por sus papeles en las series Heartstopper y Los hombres del S.A.S., además de la película Pobres criaturas o el videojuego Elden Ring, donde le puso voz a Messmer. Ahora, apunta muy alto para dar un salto en su carrera y pasara a ser el siguiente 007. Eso sí, la fuente matiza que el acuerdo aún no está cerrado y todo podría cambiar en las próximas semanas.
El próximo actor de James Bond, más cerca que nunca
Durante mucho tiempo se ha especulado con qué actor tomará el relevo de Daniel Craig y será el nuevo James Bond. Por los titulares del mundo entero han desfilado varios nombres muy potentes, desde Idris Elba hasta Tom Holland, pasando por Glen Powell. De hecho, hubo un rostro muy repetido a lo largo de diferentes épocas, el de Aaron Taylor-Johnson. Varios incluso dieron por hecho que su fichaje se cerraría tarde o temprano.
Pero con el nuevo rumbo tomado por Amazon y por Denis Villeneuve, todos esos nombres parecen haber quedado atrás. Ahora, la compañía debe decidir de una vez por todas si Jack Barton es el actor que buscan como James Bond o si se decantan por alguno de los otros intérpretes mencionados. Lo cierto es que, sea quien sea, generará debate y mucha expectación.

articles.title: Want to imagine a better future? Write a poem
articles.text:
This roundup of The Conversation’s environment coverage was first published in our award-winning weekly climate action newsletter, Imagine.
At school, I was told by my teachers I wasn’t allowed to take art A-level alongside biology and chemistry. I’ve always regretted listening to them. The crossover between the arts and sciences fascinates me. The space where creative thinking mixes with rational logic to problem solve in fresh and innovative ways. Many researchers agree that this is where the magic lies.
Here at The Conversation, I love finding new ways to communicate the climate story on a daily basis with expert insight from academics at the forefront of scientific discovery. So I was delighted to discover that others agree and spend their time researching these interdisciplinary connections – finding unusual ways to convey facts or interactive ways to engage communities and inspire action beyond the traditional, often dry, approaches.
In 2025, I started working closely with my colleague, Anna Walker, the brilliant senior arts editor at the UK edition of The Conversation. We have developed our climate storytelling strand of content and together we launched The Conversation’s Climate Poetry Award 2026, open to all academics based in the UK and Ireland. Entries close on September 1 2026 (11.59pm BST).
Don’t have time to read about climate change as much as you’d like?
Get a weekly roundup in your inbox instead. Every Wednesday, The Conversation’s environment editor writes Imagine, a short email that goes a little deeper into just one climate issue. Join the 50,000+ readers who’ve subscribed so far.
So what makes a climate poem?
As poet Sam Illingworth, a professor at Edinburgh Napier University, explains, “poetry has a profound ability to help reframe global issues, taking obscure concepts and couching them in language that is both intimate and familiar”. Poetry can help personalise the problem and reimagine solutions.
And that is possible in just 17 syllables if you write a haiku, a form of poetry that originated in Japan in the 17th century. As Illingworth explains, every haiku, by definition, is about nature and carries a kigo, a single seasonal reference: a flower, a fruit, an animal, a festival that fixes the poem in one season.
The best haikus have a kireji, a cutting word or punctuation that pivots the poem. “That final ingredient, the turn, is the reason the haiku is so well suited to climate,” writes Illingworth. “A haiku builds a scene and then breaks it. Things are one way, and then they are another. Climate change has exactly that shape, which means the form itself can carry the science.”
A shift can happen in a moment – without degrees or decades. And just as the turn can focus on climate collapse, so too can it highlight recovery.
The essence of seasons
Jasmin Kirkbride at the University of East Anglia and Paul Chambers at the University of Bristol have been analysing how English-language haiku reflect the changing climate over the past 30 years.
“Haiku are about intense moments of perception,” they describe. While flying insect populations have crashed and habitats have been lost, the frequency of heatwaves, floods and other extreme weather have all increased.
“Yet, these changes emerge in a strange fashion,” write Kirkbride and Chambers. “It’s hard to write about nature’s losses, and writers tend to do so unconsciously. Rather than tracking population declines in concrete terms, then, the language used around certain species has altered, becoming soaked in grief.”
They also noticed fewer mentions of curlews or butterflies in haiku, and out-of-place seasonal signs such as snowdrops in December rather than February.
Climate is a communication challenge
In poetry, speculation might help us make sense of what it means to live with an uncertain climate future, according to Heena Dave, a research fellow at the University of Stirling.
“Scientific knowledge might give us the foundations for understanding what futures are possible, but speculation provides a means to explore possible futures,” writes Dave, who argues that poetry gives us a language to express what living through those futures might mean. “The power of poetry lies in making us pay attention to a sound, a place, an object or something changing around us.”
Dave works closely with school leaders as they explore their hopes, worries and uncertainties about climate change through the process of writing speculative poems. She has found that writing poems helps them process their complex emotions, memories and fears. “School leaders can then consider what might be demanded of their leadership as climate change increasingly affects their schools, communities, children and young people.”
So try jumping a decade ahead. Imagine how something everyday and ordinary might fare in a climate-changed world, start with what you notice and tune into your senses. Your words might surprise you.
A poem with atmospheric powers
One poem has had a particularly direct effect on greenhouse gas emissions.
For three years, In Praise of Air by Simon Armitage hung on an exterior wall above the busy A57 in Sheffield, UK, as part of a collaborative project with physical chemistry professor Tony Ryan. This poem was printed on a 20m-tall banner coated in titanium dioxide.
“When light shines on this photocatalyst, the electrons in the material are rearranged and become more reactive. They break the oxygen in the air apart to make two oxygen free radicals,” explains Joanna Gavins, a professor in English language and literature at the University of Sheffield. “In turn, these react with water to make peroxide, which oxidises pollutants in the atmosphere, making harmless molecules that can be washed away.” In those three years, the poem removed around two tonnes of nitrogen oxide – the toxic gas emitted in exhaust fumes which causes lung disease – from the surrounding environment.
In need of more inspiration? Check out some of our favourite climate poems and watch Sam Illingworth’s climate poetry masterclass.
You can enter your climate poem online here. Shortlisted entries will be published in an ebook by The Conversation UK in the autumn. The winner will be hosted for five days at the Little Goat Barn Writing Retreat, in the peaceful and beautiful countryside of the Vale of Conwy in North Wales courtesy of The Ruppin Agency.

articles.title: „Speicher voll" – der teuerste Hinweis auf deinem Smartphone
articles.text:
Speicher voll? Fünf smarte Wege, das Beste aus deinen Geräten herauszuholen
Schöne neue Welt: Wir teilen Urlaubsfotos noch vor Ort mit Freunden, laden das neue Lieblingsspiel direkt aus dem Store und drehen spontan ein Video in 4K. Dann erscheint plötzlich eine Meldung, die niemand sehen will: „Speicher voll“. Wer besonders knapp an freiem Speicher ist, kann unter Umständen nicht einmal mehr die Kamera oder Messenger-App öffnen. Also beginnt das große Aufräumen: Apps auslagern, alte Videos durchsehen, Screenshots und doppelte Dateien löschen. Das kostet Zeit und Nerven.
Das Problem kommt nicht von ungefähr. Der Datenverbrauch wächst rasant und mit ihm der Bedarf an Speicherplatz.¹ Smartphone-Kameras machen bessere Fotos, die wiederrum mehr Speicherplatz verbrauchen. Eine Minute 4K-Video kann schnell 400 MB belegen.² Aufwendige Spiele füllen mehrere Gigabyte. Gleichzeitig liegen laut einer Bitkom-Studie rund 167 Millionen alte Handys ungenutzt in deutschen Haushalten – viele davon ersetzt, obwohl sie noch funktionierten.³ Dabei lässt sich das Speicherproblem oft einfacher und günstiger lösen als mit einem Neugerät. Die richtigen Speicherlösungen können die Nutzungsdauer von Laptops, Smartphones und Konsolen verlängern.
1. Der Laptop streikt
Für viele ist der Laptop das wichtigste Arbeitsgerät. Speicherprobleme sind hier besonders ärgerlich: Updates bleiben hängen oder lassen sich gar nicht erst herunterladen, Programme starten quälend langsam. Wer kein gutes Ordnungssystem hat, steht beim Löschen von Daten schnell vor einer Mammutaufgabe.
